body:
Why is hydrogen difficult to store?

Hydrogen contains a large amount of chemical energy relative to its mass, but it is an extremely light gas with low density at ordinary temperature and pressure. Consequently, a given mass of hydrogen occupies much more space than many familiar fuels.

For example, approximately 1 kg of hydrogen gas occupies more than 11 m3 at ordinary atmospheric pressure and room temperature. The difficulty is therefore not a lack of energy per kilogram, but a lack of energy per unit volume.

High energy per unit mass does not mean high energy per unit volume. Hydrogen's low density explains why compression, liquefaction and chemical carriers are considered for storage and transport.

Compressed hydrogen gas

One method is to store hydrogen in specially designed high-pressure cylinders or tanks. Compression places more hydrogen into a given volume. Vehicle storage systems commonly use pressures such as 350 bar or 700 bar, depending on the application.

Compressed hydrogen can be moved in cylinder arrangements or tube trailers. Pipelines can also transport hydrogen where suitable infrastructure exists. However, compression consumes energy, high-pressure tanks add cost and mass, and pipelines must be compatible with hydrogen service.

Liquid hydrogen

Hydrogen can be stored as a liquid at extremely low temperatures. At approximately atmospheric pressure, its boiling point is about −252.8°C. Storage therefore requires cryogenic equipment and effective insulation.

Liquid hydrogen occupies much less space than hydrogen gas at ordinary pressure, making it useful for certain high-volume transport requirements. However, liquefaction requires substantial energy. Some liquid hydrogen may also evaporate as heat enters a storage vessel; this is called boil-off.

Modern liquefaction processes can consume more than 30% of hydrogen's energy content. That figure describes the energy burden of liquefaction, not a universal loss of 30% of the hydrogen itself.

Chemical carriers and other storage methods

Instead of transporting hydrogen only as pure hydrogen, it can be converted into a hydrogen-containing chemical such as ammonia (NH3). Ammonia can be transported using suitable infrastructure and may either be used as a product or processed to recover hydrogen. Conversion and recovery require energy and equipment.

Hydrogen can also be stored in certain solid materials, including metal hydrides, which absorb hydrogen under suitable conditions and release it when conditions change. Such systems have their own weight, cost and operating limitations.

Transport choices depend on distance and quantity

There is no single transport method that is best in every situation. Producing hydrogen near a fertiliser plant or refinery can reduce the need for long-distance movement. Large and concentrated demand may justify dedicated pipelines. Smaller or dispersed requirements may use compressed-gas delivery, while some long-distance movements may favour liquid hydrogen or hydrogen-derived products.

Green ammonia is particularly relevant to ports and international trade because it is both an industrial product and a potential carrier of hydrogen. However, ammonia is chemically different from pure hydrogen and has its own toxicity and handling hazards.

Safety requirements

Hydrogen is flammable and can leak through small openings. It requires suitable containment, ventilation, monitoring and handling practices. High-pressure gas introduces pressure-related hazards; liquid hydrogen introduces extreme-cold hazards.

Some metals can lose toughness in hydrogen service, a problem known as hydrogen embrittlement. Equipment materials and operating procedures must therefore be selected for hydrogen compatibility.

These risks do not mean that hydrogen cannot be used safely. They mean that hydrogen systems require appropriate standards and controls, just as conventional fuel systems do.

Prelims focus

  • Hydrogen has high energy per unit mass but low energy per unit volume at ordinary pressure.
  • Compressed hydrogen storage can use pressures of 350 bar or 700 bar in vehicle applications.
  • Liquid hydrogen requires temperatures near −253°C at atmospheric pressure.
  • Boil-off is the evaporation of liquid hydrogen caused by heat entering its storage system.
  • Ammonia is a hydrogen-containing chemical carrier, not pure hydrogen.
  • Trap: Liquefaction improves storage density but does not eliminate energy costs or storage losses.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrogen Storage, sections Why Advance Hydrogen Storage Technologies? and How Hydrogen Storage Works? (updated 13 October 2026); U.S. Department of Energy, Liquid Hydrogen Delivery, sections Liquefaction and Liquid Tankers (updated 8 June 2026); Centre for High Technology, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Green Hydrogen, sections Hydrogen Storage and Hydrogen Transport, January 2025.]

title: Hydrogen Storage, Transportation and Safety

body:
Why are industrial applications important?

Hydrogen is already used in major industries. Much of this hydrogen has traditionally been produced using fossil fuels. Replacing it with green hydrogen can reduce emissions from the hydrogen-production stage while preserving hydrogen's chemical function.

The distinction between existing hydrogen demand and new hydrogen applications is useful. Fertiliser manufacture and petroleum refining already consume hydrogen. Hydrogen-based steelmaking is an important emerging application for replacing a carbon-intensive process.

Ammonia and nitrogen fertilisers

Ammonia (NH3) is produced by combining nitrogen and hydrogen. Nitrogen can be obtained from air, while hydrogen is supplied from a hydrogen-production process. The overall chemical reaction is:

N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3

Ammonia is a basic raw material for many nitrogen fertilisers. For example, urea is manufactured from ammonia and carbon dioxide. When the hydrogen used to make ammonia comes from an eligible green-hydrogen process, the resulting ammonia may be called green ammonia, subject to applicable product standards.

Using green hydrogen changes the way the hydrogen feedstock is obtained. It does not change the fact that ammonia contains nitrogen and hydrogen or that urea is a distinct fertiliser product manufactured from ammonia.

Hydrogen is not a nitrogen fertiliser. Hydrogen combines with nitrogen to make ammonia, and ammonia is then used to manufacture products such as urea.

Petroleum refining

Petroleum refineries use hydrogen for several chemical operations. In hydrodesulphurisation, hydrogen participates in reactions that remove sulphur from petroleum streams. Removing sulphur helps produce cleaner-burning fuels and meet fuel-quality requirements.

Hydrogen is also used in hydrocracking, where heavier hydrocarbon molecules are converted into lighter, more useful petroleum products under suitable conditions.

Replacing fossil-derived hydrogen with green hydrogen can reduce the emissions associated with supplying hydrogen to a refinery. However, petrol, diesel and other fossil-derived products still contain carbon and produce carbon dioxide when burned. Green hydrogen in refining does not make the final petroleum fuels carbon-free.

Iron and steel

Producing iron from iron ore requires the removal of oxygen from iron oxides. This process is called reduction. Conventional ironmaking often relies on carbon-containing reducing agents, resulting in carbon dioxide emissions.

In suitable direct reduced iron (DRI) processes, hydrogen can act as a reducing agent. When hydrogen removes oxygen from iron oxide, water is formed at that reduction stage. Green hydrogen can therefore reduce reliance on fossil-based reducing agents.

This does not mean that every steel plant can switch to hydrogen without changes. The route must be technically suitable, and the overall emissions also depend on the electricity and other inputs used across the plant.

Comparing the 3 applications

IndustryMain role of hydrogenPotential benefit of green supply
FertilisersFeedstock for ammoniaLower emissions from obtaining hydrogen for ammonia production
Petroleum refiningSulphur removal and hydrocrackingLower emissions from refinery hydrogen supply
Iron and steelReducing agent in suitable DRI processesLess dependence on carbon-based reduction

Prelims focus

  • Ammonia has the formula NH3 and is made from nitrogen and hydrogen.
  • Urea is a nitrogen fertiliser manufactured using ammonia and carbon dioxide.
  • Green ammonia can be produced using green hydrogen as its hydrogen feedstock.
  • Hydrodesulphurisation uses hydrogen to help remove sulphur from refinery streams.
  • Hydrogen can act as a reducing agent in suitable direct reduced iron processes.
  • Trap: Green hydrogen used inside a refinery does not make petrol or diesel carbon-free.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, section Applications of Green Hydrogen, 28 October 2026; International Energy Agency, Global Hydrogen Review 2026, Executive Summary, sections on traditional hydrogen demand and refining and chemical uses, June 2026; Centre for High Technology, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Green Hydrogen, sections Hydrogen in Industries and Role of Green Hydrogen in Decarbonisation, January 2025.]

title: Industrial Applications: Fertilisers, Petroleum Refining and Steel

body:
How does a hydrogen fuel cell work?

A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of hydrogen into electricity through an electrochemical reaction. Hydrogen is supplied to one electrode and oxygen from air to the other. The reaction produces electricity, water and heat.

The overall reaction is:

2H2 + O2 → 2H2O + energy

Unlike an electrolyser, a fuel cell does not use electricity to split water. It uses hydrogen to generate electricity. In a fuel-cell electric vehicle, this electricity powers an electric motor.

Transport applications

Hydrogen fuel cells may be used in suitable buses, trucks, trains and other vehicles. Potential advantages include relatively quick refuelling and the ability to carry stored fuel for longer journeys. These advantages must be considered alongside the availability of refuelling stations, storage equipment, safety arrangements and overall operating cost.

Hydrogen can also be used in specially adapted internal combustion engines. A hydrogen engine burns the fuel, while a fuel cell produces electricity electrochemically. Hydrogen combustion does not directly produce carbon dioxide from hydrogen, but high-temperature combustion in air can produce nitrogen oxides. These 2 technologies should not be treated as identical.

For ships, hydrogen-derived fuels such as green ammonia and green methanol are being considered. Green methanol requires a suitable carbon source in addition to hydrogen. Their practical use depends on compatible engines or conversion systems, fuel availability and safe port infrastructure.

Can hydrogen store excess solar and wind energy?

Solar and wind generation varies with sunlight and wind conditions. When suitable renewable electricity is available, an electrolyser can convert some of it into hydrogen for storage.

Stored hydrogen may later be consumed in an industrial process or converted back into electricity through a fuel cell. This is an example of chemical energy storage.

However, converting electricity into hydrogen and then back into electricity causes energy losses at both stages. Compression, storage and delivery may require additional energy. Therefore, hydrogen storage can be useful for certain longer-duration or industrial needs, but it is generally not the most efficient way to meet every electricity-storage requirement.

Hydrogen blending with natural gas

Hydrogen can be blended into natural gas in some networks, provided that pipelines, appliances and safety arrangements are compatible. Such blending can replace part of the fossil gas supply, but permitted proportions depend on the specific infrastructure and applicable standards.

A hydrogen-natural gas blend is not the same as pure green hydrogen. It still contains natural gas, which produces carbon dioxide when burned.

Point-of-use emissions and production emissions are different. A fuel-cell vehicle using pure hydrogen produces water and heat rather than carbon dioxide at the vehicle. Its overall environmental benefit still depends on the production, storage and delivery of that hydrogen.

Prelims focus

  • An electrolyser consumes electricity to produce hydrogen; a fuel cell consumes hydrogen to produce electricity.
  • A hydrogen fuel cell combines hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, water and heat.
  • Fuel-cell vehicles use electric motors; hydrogen combustion engines burn hydrogen as fuel.
  • Hydrogen-based storage converts electrical energy into chemical energy.
  • Green ammonia and green methanol are possible hydrogen-derived fuels for shipping.
  • Trap: A fuel-cell vehicle's lack of carbon dioxide emissions at the point of use does not prove that its hydrogen was produced without emissions.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, sections Applications of Green Hydrogen and Pilot Projects, 28 October 2026; Centre for High Technology, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Green Hydrogen, sections Hydrogen in Mobility Sector and Fuel Cell Introduction, January 2025; U.S. Department of Energy, Hydrogen Storage, section Why Advance Hydrogen Storage Technologies? (updated 13 October 2026).]
